newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Witness identifies soldiers in Cyprus assault.
newsitem.headline: Witness identifies soldiers in Cyprus assault.

text.p: An English tourist on Tuesday identified in court three British soldiers as being involved in a vicious off-duty attack on a group of her friends at a Cyprus tourist resort this month.

"I saw punching and kicking then saw these men there," said Sacha Wright, referring to defendants Steven Girvan, Tim Carter and Roger Bell, sitting opposite her in a courtroom at the coastal town of Larnaca.
Wright said she saw the soldiers as Claire Harbour, 22, and 23-year-olds Barry Ford and Shane Bell were being assaulted outside a nightclub in the resort town of Ayia Napa on August 2.
The 20-year-old London tourist rejected repeated submissions from defence lawyer Tassos Katsikides that the plaintiffs provoked the attack.
"I saw these men attacking my friends then I saw their faces," she said.
Katsikides claimed Ford and Harbour picked a fight with Roger Bell, described in court as "accused four".
Shane Bell and Roger Bell are not related.

"You saw Claire and Barry talking with accused four and then as Barry was talking Claire grabbed accused four from behind. Barry was stopped from attacking the accused by another person, who was then attacked by Barry. Then another eight persons got involved in the fight," Katsikides told Wright.
"No, that is not true," Wright responded.

Servicemen Bell, 26, Carter, 20, Grivan, 20, Steven Wolstencroft, 26, and Stuart Spencer, 20, have denied charges of causing actual bodily harm to Harbour and grievous bodily harm to Ford and Shane Bell.
Spencer, charged four days after the other soldiers, was not in court. His case will be handled separately because it was filed under a separate case number.
The soldiers, stationed at the British base at Dhekelia in Cyprus, face a maximum sentence of three years in prison if found guilty.

Ford, a quantity surveyor, suffered a shattered wrist. Shane Bell, a car mechanic, needed surgery on a fractured jawbone suffered during the attack. Doctors implanted a metal plate in his jaw which will be there for life.

All three tourists, who have postponed their departure to the UK until their testimonies are heard by the court, are suing the five Britons for damages for a joint sum of up to 25,000 Cyprus pounds ($46,500).
Earlier in the trial Katsikides accused the witnesses of fabricating the story to get compensation money.

The accused are members of the 600-strong Kings Regiment based at Dhekelia. Immediately after the attack, the British bases banned visits to Ayia Napa by members of the regiment, just one month after an earlier ban was lifted.

Visit restrictions were first imposed in September 1994 after the killing of a Danish tour guide by three members of the Royal Greenjackets, which was based at Dhekelia before the Kings Regiment took its place. They are serving a life sentence in Cyprus's central prison.
Some 3,500 troops are stationed at two military bases Britain has retained in Cyprus since independence in 1960.
The trial continues on Wednesday.
($1 = 0.53 pounds)
